Content: Exponential graphs model relationships where quantities multiply or divide by a constant factor over equal intervals. Unlike linear graphs that change steadily, or quadratic graphs that form symmetrical valleys and peaks, exponential graphs showcase explosive acceleration or rapid flattening. In the real world, this math explains compounding interest in a bank account, the population boom of bacteria, or the way a new car loses value over time. Understanding this type of curve let us predict long-term trends in scenarios where change compounds.

On the SAT exam, having a visual understanding of exponential graphs is a vital skill for solving problems in the Advanced Math category. The SAT problems often require us to look at a graphed curve to identify its matching algebraic model or determine how changes to a real-world scenario will alter the graph's behavior. Learning to decode the structure of an exponential graph helps us eliminate answer choices without the need for tedious calculations.

The first distinct type of graph that we must be able to recognize is exponential growth. This occurs when the base `b` in the standard equation `y=ab^x` is greater than `1`. On the coordinate plane, a graph of exponential growth starts flat on the left side and curves sharply upward as it moves to the right, growing steeper with every step. On the other hand, exponential decay occurs when the base `b` is a number between `0` and `1`. A graph of exponential decay starts high on the left and plunges downward as it moves to the right, flattening out as the input increases.

The absolute most critical geometric feature of an exponential graph is the asymptote. An asymptote is an invisible, horizontal boundary line that the exponential curve approaches closer and closer, but never actually crosses or touches. For the basic parent function `y=b^x`, this horizontal asymptote sits perfectly on the x-axis (`y=0`). Even if you raise a positive fraction to a massive power, it will get infinitely small but never truly become zero. On the SAT, this boundary line shifts up or down based on the constant added to the end of the equation, following the template `y=ab^x+k`. Here, the line `y=k` defines the exact location of the horizontal asymptote.

When working through the SAT exam, these concepts allow us to better solve problems visually. For example, when presented with graph and asked to identify the correct equation, our first move should be to look at the direction of the curve to determine if it represents growth or decay. This visual features tells us whether the base should be greater than `1` or a smaller decimal value. A surefire next steps is to check the horizontal asymptote of the graph. If the graph flattens out along the line `y=3`, we can eliminate any answer choices without `+3` at the end of the equation. By letting the direction of the curve and its asymptote guide problem-solving, we can effectively break down problems with advanced exponentials.
